title: Sarcopenia in patients with lung cancer: frequency, severity and implications - a mixed methods study
summary:
The human ageing process is not only evident in the skin and hair, for example, but also in the muscles. From the age of 50, the muscles lose around 1 to 2 per cent of their mass every year if no countermeasures are taken. Muscle mass is always accompanied by a loss of muscle function and a loss of strength and speed. The condition in which the loss of muscle mass becomes pathological is called sarcopenia. Sarcopenia becomes a burden when it restricts physical independence and a threat when it increases the risk of falling. Caution! Muscle loss also affects overweight people, but you can't see it at first.

In healthy people, age-related muscle loss is a slowly progressing process. According to current estimates, around half of people over the age of 80 have either a preliminary stage or full-blown sarcopenia. If people suffer from chronic diseases such as heart failure, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) or cancer, the process of muscle loss is often much faster and sarcopenia occurs earlier. Special examinations for muscle strength and function (e.g. hand strength measurement and stand-up test) are an important part of recognising sarcopenia. We are currently pursuing the goal of integrating simple examination methods into everyday clinical treatment in order to alleviate the additional burden that sarcopenia can place on our patients. Once the diagnosis has been established, countermeasures can be initiated, preferably at an early stage.

Sarcopenia is diagnosed with simple, non-stressful examinations: a hand dynamometer and the stand-up test record muscle strength and function and a BIA (bioelectrical impedance analysis) scale analyses the body's tissue components. Both take just a few minutes and usually provide reliable data for diagnosing sarcopenia.
conditions: Muscle wasting and atrophy, not elsewhere classified

interventions.name: Single-arm study among patients with pulmonary carcinoma starting cyclic therapy at the Department of Respiratory Medicine of the Nuremberg General Hospital.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Patients with all forms of lung cancer who are being treated with chemotherapy, chemoimmunotherapy, radiochemotherapy (NSCLC) or oral tumor therapy with so-called "small molecules".
Exclusion criteria:
- Presence of a cardioverter defibrillator or pacemaker
- Presence of psychological or physical impairments that do not allow study participation
- language skills too poor to give informed consent
